t: What To Do When A Student Refuses To Go To Time-Out o-time-out/
q: You see, difficult students in particular have an acute sense of fairness. And so if the way you manage your classroom is unfair, or perceived to be unfair, then it isn’t at all unusual to experience at times aggressive pushback.
If a student breaks a classroom rule, but doesn’t believe he did anything wrong, then there is a good chance he’ll become defiant.

Teachers who have their rules and consequences on a sliding scale, open to their whims, biases, and interpretations, struggle mightily with classroom management—because it’s unfair, and students know it.

Say, “Before you make that choice I’m going to give you two minutes to think about it. If after two minutes, you’re still sitting here, then I’m going to prepare a letter for you to take home to your parents.

And when a student knows it’s his choice, and that he’s not going to get any coaxing or prodding from you, or get even the slightest rise out of you, then it’s a near certainty that he’s going to quietly stand and take himself to time-out.
x: Linsin examines why students sometimes refuse to go to time-out, arguing that defiance is often a signal of underlying classroom management problems rather than simple insubordination.

He identifies four root causes: students not fully understanding the classroom management plan, teacher inconsistency, friction between teacher and student, and uncertainty about whether a rule was actually broken.

t: 6 Powerful, Soul-Searching Things To Say To Difficult Students difficult-students/
q: It is both a statement of fact and a challenge. And coming from someone they respect, four little words never said so much.
Through their words and actions, most teachers communicate to difficult students that their misbehavior is who they are, all but guaranteeing that poor behavior will not only continue, but get worse.
Difficult students are used to receiving heavy praise for modest improvement, and so this statement can come as a shock.
Because they’ve known so many of them, because they’ve been manipulated, coddled, indulged, and falsely praised ten times over, difficult students can pick a phony a mile away.
So when you appear unexpected, like a guardian angel from on high, and deliver the message they most need to hear… It will echo in their head long after you’ve turned and walked away.

t: How Best To Inform Students Of A Consequence https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2012/03/17/how-best-to-inform-students-of-a-consequence/
q: Whether you’re giving a warning, a time-out, or a letter to take home, the key is to inform them in a way that takes the focus off you—the mere deliverer of the news—and places the responsibility solely with them.
Let your agreed-upon consequence be the only consequence. Refrain from adding a talking-to, a scolding, or your two-cents worth.
A referee’s job is to enforce rules, not mediate disagreements—which makes being fair, consistent, and composed a lot easier.
As soon as you’ve informed the misbehaving student what rule was broken and the consequence, turn your attention back to what you were doing without skipping a beat.

Because if after receiving a consequence your students blame you, or become angry with you, then the consequence will be ineffective. They must see that they alone bear the responsibility for their misbehavior.
x: The interaction of informing a student of a consequence should take no more than 10-15 seconds before the teacher moves on.
Linsin argues that the manner in which a teacher delivers a consequence is as important as the consequence itself, since it determines whether responsibility lands with the student or the teacher.

t: 5 Ways To Be A Calmer, More Effective Teacher https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2012/03/10/5-ways-to-be-a-calmer-more-effective-teacher/
q: Because a tightly wound teacher translates to a tension-filled classroom—the kind of tension visitors can feel tingling in their sensory receptors the moment they enter your classroom.
Now decide that no matter what happens that day, no matter how crazy or how alarming, you will not lose your composure. And guess what? You won’t.
By slowing your movements to an easier-going, more graceful pace, your mind will slow down as well—becoming less distracted, more observant, and better able to respond to your students.
It’s remarkable what a few long, slow breaths can do. Almost immediately, blood pressure drops, your expression softens, and tension drains from your body.
Excitability in students is a major source of misbehavior, and in nearly every circumstance, teachers are to blame.
x: A teacher's own tension and stress translate directly into a more excitable, unfocused, and misbehavior-prone classroom.
Deciding, before the school day starts, not to lose composure regardless of what happens is presented as a simple but highly effective technique used by professional athletes.
Physically slowing one's pace and movements is said to calm the mind as well, improving observation and responsiveness.
Regular deep breathing throughout the day is offered as a fast, physiological way to reduce tension for both teacher and students.

q: You see, exceptional classroom management is knowledge based, not effort based.
Done right, classroom management should feel liberating. In large part, this feeling of liberation comes from what you don’t have to do.

To completely and blissfully rid yourself of the above methods, and to create the classroom you’ve always wanted, you must learn the classroom management principles, strategies, and solutions that are proven to work over time.
Look through the archives. Peruse the categories. Take careful notes. And then put what you learn into practice—one simple strategy at a time—until it becomes second nature.
The results will exceed your expectations. Your confidence will soar. And the weight of 50 grand pianos will slide gently off your shoulders.
